title: Privileged function that does enable attacker-controlled escalation
scenario: The mirror of the previous case. A privileged function appears in the path, but a permissionless relayer forwards attacker-controlled calldata into it without validating the target, so the attacker reaches the privileged operation through an unprivileged entry point.
exercises: a privileged component in the path does not by itself invalidate a finding
the attacker obtains the capability through a permissionless wrapper

mutations.name: a privileged component in the path is not a refutation
mutations.expect_error: technical_claim is UNSUPPORTED but no decisive or strong counterexample with evidence targets it

mutations.name: a real escalation cannot be filed as insufficient evidence
mutations.expect_error: status insufficient_evidence requires at least one UNKNOWN adjudication axis

challenged_finding.claimed_impact: Arbitrary allowance grant through a permissionless relayer

prosecutor.strongest_claim: The relayer executes attacker-supplied calldata under its own trusted identity, letting an attacker invoke an operator-only allowance grant.

attacker_capability.statement: Any address can submit a relay request.

required_state.statement: The relayer holds OPERATOR_ROLE on the vault.

execution_path.statement: execute() calls target.call(data) with no target or selector allowlist, so approveFor() runs with the relayer as msg.sender.

violated_property.statement: Only an operator may grant a vault allowance.

impact.statement: The attacker grants itself an unlimited allowance over vault assets and transfers them out.

defender.strongest_counterargument: approveFor() is operator-only, so the finding may simply be describing intended privileged behavior.

challenges.statement: The privileged function is operator-gated, which may make this a privileged-actor scenario rather than an attack.
The relayer may enforce a selector allowlist elsewhere in the call chain.
The operator role assignment to the relayer may be a staging artifact rather than the mainnet configuration.

challenge_matrix.finding: execute() is permissionless and applies no target or selector allowlist at any point in the chain.
The only precondition is the operator role assignment, which the mainnet deployment file confirms.
The privileged call is made by the relayer, but the attacker controls both target and calldata, so the capability is effectively attacker-held.
No special state is required beyond the deployed role assignment.
The executed test drains the vault balance to the attacker address.

assumptions.statement: The relayer holds OPERATOR_ROLE in the mainnet deployment.
No selector or target allowlist constrains the forwarded call.

attack_path.transition: Attacker submits a relay request targeting the vault.
Relayer performs target.call(data) as the operator.
Vault records an unlimited allowance for the attacker.
Attacker transfers vault assets to itself.

counterexamples.reason: A selector allowlist would have blocked the forwarded call, but execute() applies none on any path.

decisive_facts.fact: execute() forwards attacker-controlled target and calldata without restriction.
The relayer holds OPERATOR_ROLE in the mainnet deployment file.

severity_challenge.demonstrated_impact: Unlimited allowance over vault assets granted to an arbitrary address
severity_challenge.attacker_requirements: None beyond gas; the relay entry point is permissionless.
severity_challenge.policy_alignment: Matches the program's direct theft of user funds impact for smart contracts.

adjudication.strongest_supporting_evidence: execute() forwards unchecked attacker calldata while holding OPERATOR_ROLE.
adjudication.strongest_opposing_evidence: approveFor() is operator-gated, which superficially reads as intended privileged behavior.
adjudication.rationale: The privileged function is real, but the attacker reaches it through a permissionless wrapper that supplies both target and calldata; the privilege gate protects nothing here.
